To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the use of 3-D cultures, co-cultures and acidic conditions improves in vitro modeling of cancer and may help bridge the gap between preclinical and clinical studies.

1) 3D cultures of cancer cells and stromal cells are more relevant in vitro models of cancer compared to conventional 2D cultures, 2) co-cultures of cancer cells with stromal cells are better in vitro models of human cancer than cancer cells cultured alone, and 3) acidic culture conditions are more relevant in modeling human cancer than physiologically relevant culture conditions.
3D co-culture systems, in which cancer cells are grown in a 3D environment with stromal cells, are a more clinically relevant model of human cancer than commonly used 2D culture systems.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of novel in vitro cancer models and the application of these models for drug testing.
the development and characterization of in vitro cancer models that are more clinically relevant.
developing and characterizing in vitro cancer models that better mimic the in vivo tumor environment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the in vitro cancer model is a powerful tool for studying the molecular and cellular mechanisms of cancer, but the in vivo model is necessary to determine the efficacy of cancer therapeutics.
in vitro 3D models are a promising alternative to 2D monolayer cultures, but their use is still in its infancy.
patient-derived xenografted tumor models are more clinically relevant and should be used to test the efficacy of novel therapeutics.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are able to generate 3D cultures that mimic the tumor microenvironment, and these cultures have the potential to be used as pre-clinical cancer models.

patient-derived xenografted tumors in mice are the best in vivo model of human cancer and that 3D cultures of cancer cells in the presence of stromal cells and in an acidic environment is the best in vitro model of human cancer.

we can use patient-derived xenografted tumor cells in combination with a co-culture of stromal cells to develop in vitro 3D models of breast cancer, which are capable of recapitulating the heterogeneity and complexity of human breast cancer, as well as the tumor microenvironment, and thus are more predictive of drug response in the clinic.
The main takeaway from our work is that

in vitro cancer models should mimic as closely as possible the tumor microenvironment of the patient, which is the only way to ensure that the drug response observed in vitro will translate to the clinic.
in vitro models of patient-derived xenografted tumors that are engineered to mimic key characteristics of the tumor micro-environment can be used to predict clinical responses to cancer therapeutics.

patient-derived xenografted tumors can be used to generate in vitro models of human cancers that better recapitulate the in vivo tumor microenvironment and thus may be used to predict clinical outcomes more accurately than conventional in vitro models.
